extracted.intended_audience: journalists, newsroom editors, and journalism scholars/students
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizes Michael Schudson's operational norms, functions, conditions, and implications for how the objectivity ideal shapes news selection and production in American journalism. Useful for evaluating or producing news consistent with the objectivity norm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cool, Detached Tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Reports must be "cool, rather than emotional, in tone."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories that cannot be told without affect are downgraded; emotional framing or overtly affective language runs counter to the objectivity ideal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Even-Handed Treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: Reports must "represent fairly each leading side in a political controversy."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories with no oppositional framing are reframed to introduce one; coverage practices favor presenting competing sides rather than endorsing a single perspective.

rubrics_metrics.name: No Authorial Comment
rubrics_metrics.description: The journalist "reports something called 'news' without commenting on it, slanting it, or shaping its formulation in any way."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists avoid authorial interpretation; stories that require interpretation are treated as riskier than those that can be presented to 'speak for themselves.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Trustworthy via Procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: "Facts here are not aspects of the world, but consensually validated statements about it."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newsworthiness and credibility depend on procedural defensibility (e.g., named sources, documentation, verifiable methods) rather than metaphysical claims about truth; emphasis on processes that validate claims publicly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distrust of the Self
rubrics_metrics.description: Objectivity is an "ideology of the distrust of the self."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters' own observations and inferences are systematically discounted unless externally certified; first-person impressions or unverified inferences are devalued unless corroborated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Group Solidarity Function
rubrics_metrics.description: Provides a shared professional identity distinguishing journalists from PR writers, partisans, and entertainers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Objectivity functions as an internal marker of who counts as a journalist and underpins professional norms and boundaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hierarchical Control Function
rubrics_metrics.description: Allows editors to standardize and supervise reporters' work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Objectivity supplies criteria and procedures that facilitate editorial oversight and uniform reporting practices across a newsroom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Articulating Profession to Outsiders
rubrics_metrics.description: Defends journalism's claim to authority against partisan, market, and government pressures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public-facing rhetoric about objectivity helps justify the newsroom's autonomy and authority to advertisers, regulators, and audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk-Mitigation Function
rubrics_metrics.description: Reduces libel exposure and political retaliation against the outlet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural emphasis (verification, balanced sourcing) serves legal and political protective purposes by minimizing accusations of bias or defamation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural Authority Function
rubrics_metrics.description: Legitimates news as the trusted record of public life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By claiming procedural objectivity, journalism positions itself as the authoritative chronicler of events and public affairs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-conscious Internal Solidarity Pursuit (Condition for Norm Emergence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists organizing as a profession helped produce the objectivity norm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Professionalization and deliberate efforts to differentiate journalism from other occupations created incentives to adopt shared norms like objectivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for Hierarchical Control (Condition for Norm Emergence)
rubrics_metrics.description: A need for editors to control reporters contributed to the emergence of objectivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organizational demands for supervision and standardization favored norms that made reporting legible and controllable by management.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need to Articulate Ideals to Outsiders (Condition for Norm Emergence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalism needed to present ideals to advertisers, regulators, and audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Articulated ideals such as objectivity helped legitimize the profession externally and secure resources and autonomy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generational Transmission Requirement (Condition for Norm Emergence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Codifying practice for new entrants was necessary for the norm to persist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Training, routines, and institutionalization ensured objectivity was taught and reproduced across generations of reporters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural Eligibility Filter (Implication for Newsworthiness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Events lacking the right procedural shape (named sources, two-sided dispute, factual specifics) are demoted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: News selection favors events that fit recognizable procedures and documentation; items without those procedural markers are less likely to be reported as news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bias Toward Institutional Events (Implication for Newsworthiness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Because objectivity requires authoritative source citations, news skews toward events covered by named officials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coverage is more likely for occurrences involving institutions and official spokespeople who can provide verifiable statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contested-Fact Aversion (Implication for Newsworthiness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories where the underlying fact is contested without an authority adjudicating tend to be deferred or framed as 'controversy' rather than reported as fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists avoid asserting contested facts absent authoritative resolution, often reframing such matters as disputes between sides.

rubrics_metrics.name: American Specificity (Cross-national Implication)
rubrics_metrics.description: Schudson notes the objectivity norm is uniquely strong in US journalism; European traditions remain more openly political.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect cross-national variance in how objectivity shapes newsworthiness; US outlets more likely to employ the procedural/neutrality standards described here.
